unit.title: Water, food and your body
unit.summary: Hydration, fuel, heat and altitude: how the body behaves on a climb.

lessons.title: How much water
lessons.objective: You can estimate water needs for a hike and read early dehydration signs.

payload.prompt: Water for four hours of moderate hiking?

explanation.correct: About half a liter per hour is the classic starting point, so roughly 2 liters.
explanation.incorrect: Needs vary with heat and effort, but half a liter per hour is a sturdy baseline.
explanation.sayThisLine: "About half a liter an hour, so two liters for this one."

payload.prompt: Which sign means you are dehydrated and should drink?

options.text: Your urine is dark yellow or brown
Your urine is clear and pale
You have a mild headache
You feel cold

explanation.correct: Dark urine means your blood is more concentrated because you are not drinking enough. A pale, clear stream means you are well hydrated.
explanation.incorrect: Urine color is the fastest check. Dark yellow or brown signals dehydration; pale is good.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My urine was dark, so I doubled my water."

payload.prompt: You are two hours in on a hot day. Which of these suggests dehydration?

options.text: Your mouth is dry and you feel thirsty
Your legs are tired
The sun is bright
Your backpack feels heavier

explanation.correct: Thirst and a dry mouth are early signals. Drink before you are very thirsty, and sip often instead of waiting.
explanation.incorrect: Tired legs come from climbing, not dehydration alone. But thirst is the body's call for water.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I felt thirsty, so I knew it was time to drink."

payload.prompt: When is the best time to drink water on a hike?

options.text: Only at lunch break
Only when you feel very thirsty
Regularly throughout the hike, and whenever you feel thirsty
All at once at the end of the hike

explanation.correct: Small sips through the hike, plus drinking when thirst calls, keep you ahead of dehydration. Let thirst guide you; do not force huge amounts either.
explanation.incorrect: Waiting until lunch, or until you are very thirsty, lets a water deficit build. Sip often and early, and drink when thirsty.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I sip every twenty minutes, not just at lunch."

payload.prompt: It is a hot day. Should you carry more water than usual?

scene.alt: Two water bottles in the sun on a hot trail, one full and one nearly empty.

explanation.correct: Heat makes you sweat more to cool your body, so you lose water faster and should carry noticeably more. Pair it with salty snacks, and drink to thirst.
explanation.incorrect: Heat increases sweat loss, it does not reduce it. Plan on more water on hot days, and know where you can refill.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Desert heat means I carry a lot more water than on a cool day."

lessons.title: Making water safe
lessons.objective: You can compare ways to treat backcountry water and name what they stop.

payload.prompt: Match the water treatment method to what it does.

pairs.definition: Forces water through a fine membrane that blocks parasites and bacteria; check if yours covers viruses
Chlorine dioxide or iodine kills most germs, but you must wait the full time on the label (hours for some parasites)
A rolling boil kills germs anywhere, but it is slow and burns fuel
Ultraviolet light inactivates germs; fast and light, but it needs batteries and clear water

distractorDefinitions: Letting water sit in the sun overnight

explanation.summary: No single method is perfect. Filters are fast and common. Chemicals are light. UV is trendy but needs power. Boiling works anywhere.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I use a squeeze filter. It's light, but I keep it from freezing."

payload.prompt: Complete the giardia facts.
payload.template: Giardia is a {{what}} that spreads through {{how}} and causes {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Giardia is a microscopic parasite spread through animal and human feces. It causes severe cramps and diarrhea, often a week or two after you drink it.
explanation.incorrect: Giardia lives in natural water, even clear water, and causes a nasty stomach illness. Treating water is how you avoid it.

payload.prompt: You reach a clear, cold mountain stream. Drink it untreated?

scene.alt: A clear, fast mountain stream running over rocks.

explanation.correct: Clear water can carry giardia, cryptosporidium and bacteria. Clarity does not mean safety, so treat backcountry water and follow park guidance.
explanation.incorrect: Even the prettiest streams can carry invisible parasites and bacteria. Treating all backcountry water prevents illness days or weeks later.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I treat everything. Even the pretty streams."

payload.prompt: What can a typical water filter remove?

options.text: All germs and all contaminants
Most bacteria and parasites, but not viruses or toxins
Only makes the water look better
Only removes visible bugs and leaves

explanation.correct: Most filters trap bacteria and parasites but not viruses or dissolved chemicals. Viruses are a smaller worry in most U.S. backcountry, but check your filter's specs and follow park guidance.
explanation.incorrect: Filters are good at parasites and bacteria but not perfect against all viruses or pollution.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My filter stops giardia and crypto, the main worries in most places. I check the specs for viruses."

lessons.title: Salt and the water trap
lessons.objective: You can explain why plain water alone can be dangerous on long hikes.

payload.prompt: Hyponatremia is rare but real. Which situation sets it up?

options.text: Drinking far more plain water than thirst asks for, for many hours, with little food or salt
Drinking to thirst and eating regular snacks
Drinking two liters over three hours on a hot climb
Sipping less water than you need

explanation.correct: Hyponatremia is low blood sodium. It usually takes very large amounts of plain water over many hours with little food. Drinking to thirst and eating salty snacks keeps you safe.
explanation.incorrect: A normal amount of water is not the problem. Hyponatremia needs a big excess of plain water over many hours with little salt. Never withhold water from a hiker who feels unwell in the heat.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I drink to thirst and eat salty snacks. I don't force plain water."

payload.prompt: Hot day, six hours out. Which drinking plan is safest?

options.text: Drink to thirst and eat salty snacks
Force down large amounts of plain water with no food or salt
Water plus electrolyte mix or sports drink
Drink soda instead of water

explanation.correct: Drinking to thirst while eating salty snacks or using electrolyte mix replaces both water and sodium. Forcing lots of plain water well beyond thirst is what sets up hyponatremia.
explanation.incorrect: Forcing plain water with no food or salt is the risky pattern, not drinking itself. Thirst plus salty food is the safe pairing.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I drop an electrolyte tab in one bottle every hot day."

payload.prompt: Hot, 8,000 feet, dizzy, nauseous and headachy. What now?

situation.narrative: You started early on a planned six-hour hike. The sun is intense. You have drunk two liters of plain water in three hours and barely touched your salty snacks.

facts.label: Water so far
facts.value: Two liters, plain, in three hours

options.label: Stop, rest in shade, sip water and eat salty snacks
options.consequence: Shade, rest and cooling ease heat strain, and water plus salty food restore fluid and sodium. If the headache and nausea do not settle within about an hour, or get worse, head down.
considerations: Two liters in three hours is not too much; these symptoms point to heat, dehydration, altitude, or a mix
Rest, shade, cooling and salty food come first
Headache and nausea at altitude that persist mean descend
Confusion, stumbling or vomiting means get help now

options.label: Turn back and descend, resting in shade as you go
options.consequence: A cautious choice, and the right one if symptoms persist. Going down helps with altitude, but walking in the heat while unwell means slow pacing and frequent shade breaks.
considerations: Descending is the reliable fix for altitude symptoms
Rest and cool down first if you feel faint
Do not hike alone if you feel unsteady

options.label: Eat a salty snack and keep going to finish the loop
options.consequence: Hard effort in heat can push heat exhaustion toward heatstroke, and climbing higher with altitude symptoms can make them worse.
considerations: Symptoms are a signal to stop, not to push through
Salty food helps, but it does not cool you or fix altitude illness
Going higher while symptomatic is risky

options.label: Stop drinking so you do not dilute your blood sodium
options.consequence: Withholding water from a hot, symptomatic hiker can worsen dehydration and heat illness. Two liters in three hours is not the overdrinking that causes hyponatremia.
considerations: Hyponatremia needs very large volumes of plain water over many hours
Keep sipping water, and add salty food
Never cut off water from someone who may be dehydrated

payload.expertNote: Dizziness, nausea and headache in heat at altitude usually mean heat strain, dehydration, altitude illness, or a mix. Two liters in three hours is not excessive. Hyponatremia is rare and takes far larger volumes of plain water; never withhold water from a symptomatic hiker.
payload.sayThisLine: "I felt dizzy in the heat, so I stopped, cooled off, ate salty snacks and got ready to head down."
payload.safetyNote: Confusion, stumbling, repeated vomiting or a worsening headache are an emergency: descend and call for help. Follow park guidance.

payload.prompt: Complete the electrolyte fact.
payload.template: Electrolytes are {{what}}, like {{ex}}, that you lose in {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Electrolytes are essential salts your body loses in sweat. Replacing them keeps your blood chemistry balanced and your muscles working.
explanation.incorrect: Electrolytes are minerals, mainly sodium and potassium. Sports drinks, salted snacks and even broth replace them.

lessons.title: Fueling the climb
lessons.objective: You can estimate calories per hour and pick sensible trail food.

payload.prompt: You are hiking steadily uphill for four hours. Roughly how many calories will you burn?

explanation.correct: Hiking burns roughly 350 to 500 calories per hour depending on pace and terrain. Four hours is around 1,400.
explanation.incorrect: The rate varies, but three to five hundred calories per hour is typical for hiking. Steeper or faster burns more.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Hiking burns about four hundred an hour, so I snack throughout."

payload.prompt: Six-hour hike: one big lunch, or small snacks all day?

scene.alt: A trail mix bag and a sandwich on a rock at a viewpoint.

choices.label: Small snacks every hour or so
One big lunch in the middle

explanation.correct: Small, frequent snacks keep your energy steady and prevent bonking. One big lunch leaves gaps where you feel weak.
explanation.incorrect: Your body burns fuel continuously, so supply it continuously. Snacking about hourly beats a single large meal.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Snack every hour, not just at lunch."

payload.prompt: Choose the words that describe good trail food.

explanation.correct: Trail snacks pack lots of calories without weighing much, and they do not spoil or crumble in a pack.
explanation.incorrect: Good trail food is dense (nuts, bars, jerky), not light and fluffy (chips, popcorn). It has to survive jostling.

payload.prompt: Which of these is a good trail snack?

options.text: Nuts and nut butter
Chocolate and energy bars
Jerky and dried fruit
All of the above

explanation.correct: Nuts, bars, chocolate, jerky and dried fruit are all great trail snacks. They are calorie-dense, shelf-stable and they pack well.
explanation.incorrect: Good trail food is calorie-dense and does not spoil. Mix salty, sweet and fatty for variety.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Tortillas and peanut butter is a solid trail lunch."

payload.prompt: Match each snack to how it holds up on trail.

pairs.definition: Calorie-dense and survives a bouncing pack
Salty protein that keeps for days
Sweet, quick energy that packs small
Bruises, wilts and spoils, and has few calories

distractorDefinitions: Melts into a mess in a warm pack and needs a fridge

explanation.summary: Good trail food is calorie-dense, durable and light. Fresh greens fail all three tests.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I bring dried fruit and nuts, not fresh stuff."

lessons.title: Hitting the wall
lessons.objective: You can spot bonking early and know how to fix it.

payload.prompt: Complete the bonking fact.
payload.template: Bonking is running low on {{fuel}}, leaving you {{feel}}. The fix is to {{fix}}.

explanation.correct: Bonking is hitting the wall: your energy stores are depleted, so you feel weak, shaky and irritable. Food and a short rest usually fix it.
explanation.incorrect: Bonking is an energy crash from not eating enough. You get slow and cranky, and food is the cure.

payload.prompt: Which of these is a sign that you are bonking?

options.text: Sudden weakness and slowness
Sudden irritability or confusion
Tunnel vision or dizziness
All of the above

explanation.correct: Bonking feels like a wall: weakness, mood changes, foggy thinking and even tunnel vision. Eat and rest. If confusion or dizziness does not clear, something else, like heat or altitude illness, may be going on.
explanation.incorrect: Bonking is an energy crash. It brings weakness, mood shifts and sometimes strange symptoms.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I started getting cranky and slow, so I knew I needed to eat."

payload.prompt: Five hours into an eight-hour hike. You are getting weak, slow and irritable. Your legs feel like lead.

situation.narrative: You had breakfast at six AM and a granola bar at hour two. You have barely eaten since, and the terrain is getting steeper.

facts.label: Snacks eaten since breakfast
facts.value: One granola bar, at hour two

options.label: Push on to the finish, you are halfway done
options.consequence: Another hour of weakness makes you slower and more irritable. Hiking on empty is dangerous and miserable.
considerations: Weak muscles make mistakes
Low energy clouds judgment
Finish without eating is a recipe for trouble

options.label: Stop, eat snacks, drink water and rest 15 minutes
options.consequence: Calories, water and a short break usually restore energy and mood within 15 to 30 minutes. If you do not feel clearly better, treat it as more than hunger and turn back.
considerations: Eating and drinking usually helps within 15 to 30 minutes
A short break helps more than you expect
If you do not improve, or feel dizzy or confused, turn around

options.label: Turn back to the trailhead
options.consequence: A cautious choice, though eating and resting first usually gets you moving again. Turn back if eating does not help.
considerations: Turning back is safe but often unnecessary
Food and rest usually fix bonking quickly
Turn back if symptoms persist after eating and resting

payload.expertNote: Bonking is usually preventable: eat small amounts often. If eating and resting do not help, or you feel dizzy or confused, something else may be wrong; turn back.
payload.sayThisLine: "I ate a few hundred calories and felt like a new person."

payload.prompt: Feeling great early on. Wait to eat until you feel weak?

scene.alt: A hiker with a snack in one hand, striding up a sunny trail.

choices.label: No, eat small amounts early and often

explanation.correct: Small, frequent snacks keep your energy steady all day. By the time you feel weak, you are already behind.
explanation.incorrect: Waiting for weakness means you are already bonking. Steady fuel beats big meals or going without.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I snack every hour now. Never bonked since."

lessons.title: When heat turns serious
lessons.objective: You can distinguish heat cramps, exhaustion and heatstroke in plain language.

payload.prompt: Complete the heat cramps fact.
payload.template: Heat cramps are painful {{what}}, often after heavy {{cause}}. Rest in shade and {{treat}}.

explanation.correct: Heat cramps are sudden, painful muscle spasms, usually in the legs, from sweat loss and low electrolytes. Rest, cool off, and sip water with salt or a sports drink.
explanation.incorrect: Heat cramps are a sign of salt and fluid loss. Stop, rest in shade, and replace water and salt before continuing.

payload.prompt: Match each heat problem to what you would see and do.

pairs.definition: Painful muscle spasms: rest in shade, sip water with salt
Weak, dizzy, nauseous, sweating heavily: stop, cool down, sip fluids
Confusion or collapse with a very hot body: call 911 and cool now

distractorDefinitions: Sunburn on exposed skin: reapply sunscreen and cover up

explanation.summary: Heat problems form a ladder. Cramps and exhaustion mean stop and cool down. Confusion or collapse is heatstroke, an emergency.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Dizzy and weak means stop and cool down. Confused means call for help."

payload.prompt: What marks heatstroke, and how is it different from heat exhaustion?

options.text: Confusion, stumbling or collapse with a very hot body: a medical emergency
The same thing, just a different name
Worse muscle cramps
More nausea and vomiting

explanation.correct: Heatstroke is life-threatening. The key sign is a change in thinking or behavior (confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, collapse) with a very hot body. Skin may be dry or still sweaty. Call emergency services and cool the person right away.
explanation.incorrect: Heatstroke is when the body's cooling fails. Any confusion in a hot, exhausted hiker is a red flag. Call for help and start cooling them; do not wait to hike out.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Confusion in the heat means call for help and cool them down, right now."

payload.prompt: Two PM, exposed canyon. Your friend is dizzy, pale and nauseous.

situation.narrative: You started at eight AM and have hiked steadily in a narrow canyon with no shade. The air temperature is 92 degrees F.

options.label: Keep hiking to the car, it is only two miles
options.consequence: Walking on in the heat with heat exhaustion can push her toward heatstroke. Two miles is a long way when her body cannot cool.
considerations: Her symptoms mean she is overheating
Continuing without rest is dangerous
Heat exhaustion can become heatstroke fast

options.label: Stop, make shade with a pack or jacket, cool her and let her sip water
options.consequence: Rest, shade, cooling (wet cloth on neck and face, fanning) and slow sips of water or electrolyte drink are the right first steps. If she is not clearly better in about 30 minutes, or gets confused, call for emergency help.
considerations: Heat exhaustion is treated with rest, shade, cooling and fluids
Confusion, stumbling or collapse means heatstroke: call 911 and cool her fast
If she improves, walk out slowly with frequent shade breaks
Do not leave her alone

options.label: Once she can walk steadily, ease back to the creek to cool off
options.consequence: Creek water is great for cooling, but rest and cool her where she is first. A mile of walking while symptomatic adds strain, so move only if she is steady, and go slowly.
considerations: Cooling in water is very effective
Start cooling before you move her
Stop and call for help if she gets worse on the way

payload.expertNote: Heat exhaustion: dizziness, weakness, nausea and heavy sweating. Heatstroke adds confusion or collapse and is an emergency: call for help and cool the person immediately. She may still be sweating, so do not wait for dry skin.
payload.sayThisLine: "We started at dawn because the canyon is dangerous by noon."
payload.safetyNote: If she becomes confused, faints or cannot drink, call 911 and cool her right away. Do not wait to walk out.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: We turned back because the heat was getting serious and I was dizzy.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She was likely showing early signs of heat illness
She was tired from walking
She was bored
She thought the heat was dangerous

payload.translation: She recognized early signs of heat illness (dizziness) and made a smart, cautious choice to turn back before it got worse.

followUps.line: Good call. Did you rest and drink water?
followUps.why: Shows you know the first aid.

followUps.line: Did you start earlier on your next trip?
followUps.why: Asks if she learned from it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Recognize that dizziness in heat is serious. Applaud the decision to turn back.

lessons.title: Going high
lessons.objective: You can explain acclimatization and recognize altitude sickness.

payload.prompt: What is altitude sickness?

options.text: Headache, nausea and fatigue from going up too fast
A cold caught at high elevation
Fear of heights
Nothing real, just laziness

explanation.correct: Altitude sickness happens when you go up faster than your body can adjust. Headache, nausea and fatigue are common above roughly 8,000 feet and can show up lower for some people. If symptoms worsen, descend.
explanation.incorrect: Altitude sickness is real: low oxygen causes headache, nausea and weakness.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I had a headache at the pass. Altitude, I think."

payload.prompt: Complete the acclimatization idea.
payload.template: Acclimatization means your body {{what}} by {{how}}, and you sleep {{sleep}} than your high point.

explanation.correct: Acclimatization is your body adjusting to lower oxygen over days. You help it by ascending gradually and sleeping lower than the highest point you reached.
explanation.incorrect: Acclimatization takes time, not effort. Slow ascent and sleeping at a lower elevation give your body room to adjust.

payload.prompt: How do you acclimatize on a mountain trip to 12,000 feet?

options.text: Drive to 12,000 feet as fast as possible
Spend a night at an intermediate elevation like 8,000 or 9,000 feet first
Run at altitude to build fitness
There is no strategy, you just go

explanation.correct: Ascending slowly with stops at intermediate elevations lets your body adapt. Sleeping lower than your high point helps most.
explanation.incorrect: Going fast causes altitude sickness. A slow ascent and sleeping at intermediate heights give your body time to adjust.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We're spending a night at 8,000 feet to acclimatize first."

payload.prompt: 10,500 feet, headache and nausea. Still hike to 12,500?

situation.narrative: You flew in yesterday and slept poorly. You woke with a headache, nausea and low energy. Today's plan climbs about 2,000 feet higher.

options.label: Hike anyway, you will feel better once you move
options.consequence: Going higher with altitude sickness can make it worse and can turn serious. Symptoms are a reason not to go up.
considerations: Do not ascend with symptoms
Exertion and height can make it worse
Feeling better while moving does not mean it is gone

options.label: Skip the climb: rest, drink water, and go no higher until symptoms clear
options.consequence: Staying at the same elevation gives your body time to adjust. Mild symptoms often ease in a day or so. Do not go higher until they are gone, and go down if they worsen.
considerations: Rest and fluids; skip alcohol
Worse headache, vomiting, confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest means descend now and get help
Ask a clinician about prevention before your next high trip

options.label: Descend to a lower town and try again later
options.consequence: Going down is the most reliable treatment, and the right call if symptoms persist or worsen. If you feel better after resting, waiting a day at this height is also reasonable.
considerations: Descending fixes altitude sickness quickly
It becomes the best choice if symptoms worsen
You can return once acclimatized

payload.expertNote: Altitude sickness tracks how fast you go up. Mild symptoms mean stop climbing and rest; worsening means descend. Confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest are emergencies. Follow medical and park guidance.
payload.sayThisLine: "I had a headache on arrival, so I rested a day instead of climbing higher."
payload.safetyNote: Never ascend with symptoms. If they worsen, or you become confused or unsteady, descend and seek medical help.

payload.prompt: You are planning a hike to 13,000 feet. What is smart preparation?

options.text: Fly in and hike the next day
Drive in gradually or spend time at intermediate elevations first
Train hard before you go
Just go, altitude is not a big deal

explanation.correct: Gradual ascent is the best prevention. Stop at intermediate elevations and sleep lower than your high point.
explanation.incorrect: Flying in and hiking immediately is a recipe for altitude sickness. Gradual ascent prevents it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We drive up slowly and sleep at eight thousand first."
